title: THEY TOLD YOU TO SOW A SEED BEFORE GOD WOULD MOVE. BUT DID JESUS EVER PUT A PRICE ON A MIRACLE?
paragraphs: THEY TOLD YOU TO SOW A SEED BEFORE GOD WOULD MOVE. BUT DID JESUS EVER PUT A PRICE ON A MIRACLE?

When prophecy becomes a transaction, desperation becomes someone else's income, and the suffering are told to pay for what Christ freely gives, we must ask a question that could expose an entire religious system: Are we honoring God with our offerings, or allowing someone to sell us what belongs to Him?
Imagine a mother sitting on the edge of her bed at two in the morning.

Her child is sick. The hospital bills are growing. The money she has left is barely enough for groceries. She has prayed until her voice has become a whisper, cried until her eyes have nothing left to give, and begged God for an answer that still hasn't come.
Then her phone lights up.
A preacher is speaking with extraordinary confidence.
"Somebody watching right now is about to receive a miracle. But God is asking you to demonstrate your faith. Sow a seed of $100. Don't delay your breakthrough."
Her heart starts pounding.
What if this is God speaking?
What if this is the answer she's been waiting for?
What if refusing to give means refusing her miracle?
She looks at her child. Then at her bank balance.
And suddenly, the question isn't whether she can afford to give.
It's whether she can afford not to.
That is where something deeply troubling can happen.
Because when someone convinces a desperate person that God's mercy is waiting on the other side of a financial transaction, they are no longer simply inviting generosity.
They may be turning human suffering into a marketplace.
And the most frightening part?
They may be doing it while holding a Bible.
Before we go further, understand something important.
This is not an attack on faithful pastors, legitimate ministries, biblical generosity, or the sacrificial support of Gospel work.
Scripture teaches believers to give. It teaches churches to support those who labor faithfully in ministry. It celebrates generosity that flows from love, gratitude, and trust in God.
And that line matters more than many people realize.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
The Holy Spirit is not for sale.
And Jesus Christ did not bleed on a Roman cross so that someone could become a middleman charging admission to His mercy.
There is a moment in the book of Acts that should make every Christian who has ever been pressured to pay for a spiritual blessing stop and think.

A man named Simon had practiced magic in Samaria. He had astonished people and attracted attention through his abilities. But when Philip proclaimed the Gospel, Simon himself professed belief and was baptized.
Later, Peter and John came to Samaria. Through their ministry, the Holy Spirit was given to believers.
Simon witnessed something extraordinary.
And he wanted that power.
Not merely to experience God's grace, but to possess the authority to impart the Spirit through the laying on of hands.
So he offered money.
Acts 8:18–19 describes his proposal.
And Peter's response was devastating.
In the original Greek of Acts 8:20, Peter declares:
«Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν»
To argyrion sou syn soi eiē eis apōleian.
In context, the words mean:
"May your silver perish with you."
Peter continues, explaining that Simon had thought he could obtain God's gift through money.
Read that again.
Peter did not negotiate a higher offering.
He did not create a special partnership level.
He did not tell Simon that a larger seed would unlock greater spiritual authority.
He rebuked him.
Why?
Because Simon had fundamentally misunderstood the nature of God's gift.
The Greek word δωρεά (dōrea), used in Acts 8:20, refers to a gift. In this passage, Peter speaks of the gift of God—something Simon had wrongly imagined could be acquired through payment.
And Peter went even deeper.
He told Simon that his heart was not right before God and called him to repent and pray for forgiveness (Acts 8:21–22).
This wasn't merely a disagreement about fundraising methods.
It was a confrontation over the corruption of spiritual desire.
Simon wanted something holy, but approached it through the logic of ownership, control, and purchase.
And that same temptation has never completely disappeared from religious life.
Sometimes it wears expensive clothing.
Sometimes it stands beneath bright stage lights.
Sometimes it arrives in a private message promising a personal prophecy in exchange for a payment.
Sometimes it speaks gently, saying, "God showed me something about your future, but you need to release a seed first."
And sometimes it doesn't look like greed at all.
It looks like hope.
That is what makes it dangerous.
Because desperate people are often willing to sacrifice almost anything for the possibility that tomorrow might finally be different.
But what did Jesus actually teach?
In Matthew 10:8, when Jesus commissioned the Twelve and gave them authority for their mission, He instructed them to heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons.
Then He said something that should echo through every ministry that claims to operate in His name.
The Greek reads:
«δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε, δωρεὰν δότε»
Dōrean elabete, dōrean dote.
"Freely you received, freely give."
The Greek word δωρεάν (dōrean) carries the sense of freely, without payment, or gratuitously.
Jesus was not abolishing every legitimate form of financial support for ministry. In the same missionary discourse, He acknowledged that a worker deserves provision (Matthew 10:10).
But He was establishing a vital distinction.
The authority entrusted to His disciples was not a commodity to be sold.
They were servants entrusted with God's work, not merchants who owned God's power.
And that distinction remains essential.
A church may receive offerings.
A missionary may be financially supported.
A pastor may receive compensation for faithful labor.
A Christian author may sell a book.
A ministry may charge a reasonable amount for a conference, accommodation, materials, or other legitimate expenses.
None of these things automatically means someone is selling God's grace.

But when payment becomes the supposed condition for receiving a prophecy, healing, deliverance, divine favor, or access to God's supernatural power, the transaction has crossed into spiritually dangerous territory.
And you can give generously without pretending that God owes you a supernatural return.
Consider another biblical account.
In 2 Kings 5, Naaman was a powerful Syrian military commander suffering from leprosy.
He came seeking healing through the prophet Elisha.
After initially resisting the prophet's simple instructions, Naaman obeyed, washed in the Jordan, and was healed.
Overwhelmed with gratitude, he returned and offered Elisha a gift.
Elisha refused.
He declared, "As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none" (2 Kings 5:16, KJV).
That refusal is significant.
Elisha wanted Naaman to understand that his healing was the work of the living God, not a service that could be purchased from a prophet.
But the story did not end there.
Elisha's servant Gehazi saw an opportunity.
He pursued Naaman, lied about his master's intentions, and obtained silver and garments.
Gehazi attempted to profit from a moment in which God's mercy had been displayed freely.
When Elisha confronted him, the consequences were severe (2 Kings 5:20–27).
Notice the contrast.
Naaman received healing without purchasing it.
Gehazi pursued payment through deception and greed.
And the servant who tried to enrich himself through God's work became a warning about the corruption of spiritual ministry.
This does not mean every gift offered to a prophet was sinful. Scripture records occasions when people brought gifts or provisions to God's servants.
The issue in Gehazi's case was his dishonesty, greed, and exploitation of a moment of divine mercy.
That distinction protects us from two opposite errors.
We must not condemn every financial gift to a ministry.
But neither should we excuse religious manipulation merely because someone calls the payment an offering.
Now imagine that mother again.
The one staring at her phone while her child sleeps.
Suppose she gives her last money because someone told her that God would withhold healing unless she sowed a seed.
And suppose her child does not recover as she hoped.
What happens to her faith?
Perhaps someone tells her she didn't give enough.
Perhaps someone tells her she doubted.
Perhaps she is told that another, larger offering is required to break the resistance.
And now she is carrying more than financial loss.
She is carrying shame.
She begins wondering whether God is disappointed in her.
Whether her prayers were inadequate.
Whether her child's suffering is somehow the result of her failure to satisfy a spiritual demand.
Do you see the cruelty that can hide inside religious language?
A person already crushed by suffering is made to believe that God's compassion must be financially activated.
But Scripture gives us no authority to tell a suffering mother that a payment will guarantee her child's healing.
God can heal.
Christians are invited to pray for the sick (James 5:14–16).
We can ask boldly for His mercy.
Yet we must not promise what God has not promised, claim certainty where Scripture does not give it, or turn unanswered prayer into an accusation against the sufferer.
Even the apostle Paul prayed repeatedly about his thorn in the flesh, and the Lord answered by emphasizing the sufficiency of His grace rather than removing the affliction (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
Paul was not told to purchase deliverance.
He was taught to depend on Christ.
God's grace is not measured by how quickly our suffering disappears.
And a person who remains sick, poor, grieving, or exhausted has not thereby been abandoned by Jesus.
That truth may be the very thing someone reading this needs tonight.
Because perhaps you have given.
And given again.
You have emptied your savings, believed the promises, attended the services, followed the instructions, and waited for the breakthrough someone assured you would come.
And when it didn't, you blamed yourself.
You thought your faith wasn't strong enough.
You wondered whether God had closed His ears to your prayers.
But hear the words of Jesus in Matthew 11:28:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (KJV)
He did not say, "Come after you have paid."
He did not say, "Come when your offering reaches the required amount."
He said, "Come unto me."
The invitation is rooted in His mercy.
And the heart of Christianity is not a transaction in which sinners purchase divine attention.
It is the Gospel of a Savior who came to rescue people who could never save themselves.
The prophet Isaiah had already used striking language to describe God's gracious invitation.
In Isaiah 55:1, the Hebrew text includes these words:
«לְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ בְלוֹא־כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר»
Lekhu shivru belo-khesef uvelo mekhir.
The phrase communicates the invitation to come and obtain what is offered without money and without price.
In its original context, Isaiah is calling thirsty and needy people to receive God's gracious provision and listen to His life-giving covenant invitation.
The passage is not teaching that food, ministry buildings, or every human service must always be free.
It is portraying the generosity of God, whose saving invitation cannot be reduced to commercial exchange.
And that message finds its deepest fulfillment in the grace revealed through Jesus Christ.
Because at Calvary, the greatest need of humanity was not answered by a fundraising campaign.
It was answered by a crucified Savior.
Our sin was real.
Our guilt was real.
Our separation from God was real.
And no amount of money could purchase forgiveness.
No donation could erase our rebellion.
No religious performance could make us righteous before a holy God.
Yet Jesus, the sinless Son of God, gave Himself for sinners.
First Peter 1:18–19 declares that believers were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
Think about that.
The price of your redemption was never something you could afford.
And the One who paid it did not send you an invoice.
This is the scandal of grace.
The guilty are offered forgiveness through the innocent One who suffered for them.
The spiritually bankrupt are invited to receive the riches of God's mercy.
The sinner who cannot purchase salvation is called to repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
And the person who has been manipulated in God's name is invited to discover the character of the true Shepherd.
Not a salesman of miracles.
Not a collector of desperation.
Not a religious gatekeeper who profits from fear.
But Jesus Christ.
The Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11).
Now, there is another side of this conversation that we cannot ignore.
Because some people hear messages like this and conclude that Christians should never give money to churches or ministries.
That conclusion is also unbiblical.
The New Testament clearly affirms the material support of Gospel ministry.
In 1 Corinthians 9:14, Paul writes that the Lord ordained that those who preach the Gospel should live from the Gospel.
In Galatians 6:6, believers are instructed to share good things with those who teach them the Word.
Philippians 4:15–18 records the generosity of the Philippian believers toward Paul's ministry, which he describes using the language of a pleasing sacrifice to God.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 establishes an essential principle:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
The Greek word ἀνάγκης (anankēs) in this verse carries the sense of necessity or compulsion.
Paul is teaching generosity that is willing and heartfelt, not forced through pressure.
So biblical giving is not the problem.
Manipulative giving is.
Faithful financial support can help proclaim the Gospel, disciple believers, provide resources, meet practical needs, and sustain those serving in ministry.
But support must never be presented as a purchase of God's favor.
It may be a regular expression of generosity, stewardship, and commitment to Gospel outreach.

Christians hold different convictions about how Old Testament tithing applies under the New Covenant. What is clear is that New Testament believers are called to generosity, care for those in need, and support for faithful Gospel work.
It must never be treated as a requirement for God's blessing, a guarantee of healing, or proof that your faith is genuine.
And this matters deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
Because if we are going to speak against the commercialization of spiritual gifts, we must also hold ourselves to the same biblical standard.
We will not claim that financial support guarantees answered prayers, healing, prosperity, or special access to the Holy Spirit.
The Gospel must remain the Gospel.
Freely proclaimed.
Christ-centered.
Rooted in Scripture.
And available to those who cannot afford to contribute.
But there is something beautiful about believers freely deciding to help carry that message farther.
Not because God needs your money to be powerful.
But because Christian ministry involves real work, real time, real resources, and real opportunities to serve people.
And when believers voluntarily share in those responsibilities, they can participate in something larger than themselves.
Those resources are part of our commitment to making biblical nourishment accessible, not reserving it for people who can pay.
It is not a spiritual reward.
It is not a greater measure of God's favor.
And it is certainly not a price for prophecy, prayer, or blessing.

If you are financially struggling, please do not give out of fear, guilt, or pressure. Care for your essential needs and responsibilities. You are welcome here, and the Gospel is no less available to you.
And perhaps the most powerful thing you can do today will not cost you anything.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because somewhere among your friends is a person who has been made to believe that God will not answer unless they pay.
Somewhere there is a widow who has been pressured to give what she needs for food.
Somewhere there is a young believer who has confused a preacher's confidence with God's voice.
Somewhere there is a wounded Christian who has quietly walked away from church because spiritual manipulation convinced them that Christianity was only another way to take their money.
And somewhere there is a faithful pastor who would welcome a clear biblical distinction between honest ministry support and the sale of supposed supernatural power.
Have you ever felt pressured to give money because someone promised a prophecy, miracle, healing, or breakthrough?
You do not have to name anyone or share details you would rather keep private.
Let this become a place where people tell the truth without shame, where Scripture is taken seriously, and where those who have been hurt are not treated as weak for asking questions.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown distant from God, and even people who are still searching for the truth about Jesus.
Not everyone who needs the Gospel knows how to ask for it.
But before you leave, there is one more biblical warning we must face.
In Jeremiah 23, God confronts prophets who spoke visions arising from their own hearts rather than from His mouth.
In Ezekiel 13, false prophetic claims are exposed and condemned.
In Micah 3:11, the prophet rebukes religious leaders who judge for reward, teach for payment, and divine for money while claiming that the LORD is among them.
These passages do not establish that every financially supported minister is corrupt.
They reveal the danger of spiritual leaders who exploit their positions, speak falsely in God's name, and confuse financial advantage with faithfulness.
That warning reaches beyond ancient Israel.
Because spiritual language can sound convincing.
A person can say "The Lord told me" with tears in their eyes.
They can quote Scripture.
They can describe your pain so accurately that you feel as though heaven itself has spoken.
But the presence of religious emotion does not prove the presence of divine revelation.
The apostle John instructs believers not to believe every spirit, but to test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1).
Paul instructs the church to test everything and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21).
And Scripture gives us a clear foundation for discernment.
A claimed prophecy must not contradict God's revealed Word.
A person claiming spiritual authority must not be exempt from examination.
And no one should be allowed to use fear, financial pressure, or the promise of supernatural intervention to silence legitimate questions.
Not every prophecy claimed today is genuine simply because someone calls it prophetic.
Not every extraordinary experience is evidence that God has endorsed the person involved.
And not every ministry that requests an offering is acting dishonestly.
Discernment requires more than suspicion.
It requires truth.
It requires humility.
It requires careful attention to Scripture.
And above all, it requires keeping Jesus Christ at the center.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about finding the right person to unlock your destiny.
It is about being reconciled to God through His Son.
It is about repentance from sin.
Forgiveness through Christ.
The gift of the Holy Spirit.
A new life of obedience, faith, and love.
And a hope that remains even when circumstances do not change the way we desperately wanted them to.
Remember the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
Luke 23:39–43 records a dying man acknowledging his guilt, recognizing Jesus' innocence, and asking to be remembered when Christ came into His kingdom.
He had no opportunity to build a financial offering.
No money with which to purchase an audience.
No years left to prove his worthiness.
He simply turned to Jesus.
And Jesus promised him paradise.
That moment does not mean repentance is unnecessary. The criminal's words reveal a remarkable recognition of guilt and an appeal to Christ.
It means salvation rests upon the mercy and authority of the Savior, not upon the financial resources of the sinner.
And that is the hope of the Gospel.
The person with nothing in their wallet can come to Christ.
The person who has been deceived can come to Christ.
The person who has made terrible mistakes can come to Christ.
The person who once tried to buy God's favor can repent and come to Christ.
The person who has profited dishonestly through religion can also repent, abandon deception, make appropriate restitution, and seek God's forgiveness.
No one is beyond the call to repentance.
And no one can purchase the grace that makes forgiveness possible.
Perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you have been the desperate person reaching for a miracle.
Maybe you have been the believer who gave because you were afraid not to.
Maybe you have been the one who defended a religious leader because questioning them felt like questioning God.
Or maybe you have been tempted to measure God's approval by how much money someone gives to your ministry.
Wherever you recognize yourself, do not look away.
Bring it into the light.
Jesus does not call us to defend what is false simply because it has become familiar.
He calls us to follow Him in truth.
And truth sometimes dismantles things we once trusted.
That can hurt.
It can feel like betrayal.
It can leave us wondering what else we misunderstood.
But losing confidence in a manipulative religious system does not have to mean losing faith in Jesus Christ.
Sometimes it becomes the beginning of seeing Him more clearly.
The Jesus of Scripture is greater than the promises of a prosperity salesman.
Greater than a staged display of religious power.
Greater than a paid prophecy.
Greater than the fear that someone has convinced you to carry.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
And His Gospel is not controlled by the people who claim to represent Him.
So give, when you give, because you love God and desire to serve others.
Support faithful Gospel work when you are able and persuaded that it is worthy of support.
Examine ministries with wisdom.
Ask questions about financial integrity.
Refuse manipulation.
Pray boldly for healing without pretending that healing can be guaranteed through a donation.
Seek biblical counsel.
Test prophetic claims.
And never confuse a preacher's demand with a command from Jesus.
You do not have to buy your way into the mercy of Jesus Christ.
You come to Him in repentance and faith.
And when His grace changes you, your generosity can become an expression of gratitude rather than a payment driven by fear.
That is the difference between a marketplace and the Gospel.
One asks what you can pay to receive.
The other announces what Christ has done to save.
One makes desperate people afraid of losing their blessing.
The other points sinners toward the Savior who gave Himself for them.
And one day, when the voices of religious salesmanship have faded, the truth will remain:
The miracle you needed most was never a prophecy someone could sell you—it was a Savior who gave Himself to redeem you.
